GANs & Diffusion Models

Two ways to turn noise into data

A classifier learns to tell a 3 from an 8. A generative model learns to draw new threes. Two ideas dominate. A GAN pits a forger against a detective until the forgeries pass. A diffusion model learns to undo noise, one small step at a time. On the right are 1,500 points of pure noise. Drag the clock back from t = 100 to 0 and watch a denoiser pull them into shape.

The goal

From noise to data: a generator is a map

Every model in this chapter starts from the same trick. Noise is easy to sample: a computer can draw numbers from a bell curve all day. Data is not. So learn a function G that moves noise to where the data lives: draw z, compute x = G(z), and you have a new sample. Where G stretches space, probability is spread thin. Where G squeezes it, probability piles up. Below, the bell curve along the bottom is the noise z, and the shaded humps along the top are the real data. Drag the seven handles along the top to reshape G until what it produces (the line) matches the data.

\[ \begin{aligned} &z \sim \mathcal N(0,1),\quad x = G(z) \\ &\Rightarrow\ p_G(x) = \frac{p_z(z)}{\lvert G'(z)\rvert} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: G moves probability without creating or destroying any. The mass in a thin slice dz of noise lands in a slice |G′(z)| dz wide, so its density is divided by the stretch |G′(z)|, evaluated at the z that maps to x. A steep stretch of G spreads the noise thin; a flat stretch stacks it into a hump. In hundreds of dimensions the stretch becomes a determinant that nobody can compute for a deep network, so a GAN needs another way to compare pG with the data. That is the next section.
Say it“z is standard normal and x is G of z; the density of x is the density of z divided by the slope of G.”
JS divergence to the data
stretch G′ next to the last handle moved

The critic

A discriminator measures the gap

In high dimensions we cannot write pG down, but we can still sample from it. Goodfellow and colleagues (2014) had the key idea: train a second network, the discriminator D, to tell real samples from generated ones. For a fixed generator the best possible discriminator has a closed form, and how well it succeeds measures how far apart the two distributions are. Here the generator is a plain Gaussian. Move its centre and width and watch the best discriminator’s verdict D*(x): the probability that a sample found at x is real.

\[ D^*(x) = \frac{p_{\text{data}}(x)}{p_{\text{data}}(x) + p_G(x)} \]
Read it as: where only real data lives, D* says 1. Where only fakes land, it says 0. Where the two densities are equal it says 0.5, a coin flip. A generator has won when D* is 0.5 everywhere.
Say it“D-star of x is p-data over p-data plus p-G.”
\[ \begin{aligned} V(D^*, G) &= -\log 4 \\ &\quad + 2\,\mathrm{JSD}(p_{\text{data}} \,\Vert\, p_G) \\ \mathrm{JSD}(p\,\Vert\,q) &= \tfrac12\mathrm{KL}(p\,\Vert\,m) \\ &\quad + \tfrac12\mathrm{KL}(q\,\Vert\,m) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: V is the discriminator’s score (defined in the next section). With the best D plugged in it becomes the Jensen–Shannon divergence, where m = (p + q)/2 is the half-and-half mixture. JSD is 0 when the distributions are identical and ln 2 ≈ 0.693 when they do not overlap at all. Training G to lower V therefore drags pG towards pdata.
Say it“V at the best D is minus log four plus twice the Jensen–Shannon divergence.”
JSD (nats)
D* at the probe

Forger against detective

The GAN game, trained live

Now let both players learn. The discriminator D, a small network, is trained to output 1 on real points and 0 on fakes. The generator G, another small network that turns two noise numbers into a point, is trained to make D say 1. They take turns, one gradient step each. G never sees the data. It learns only through D’s gradient, which tells every fake point which way looks more real. Press Train and watch the background (D’s opinion) chase the fakes while the fakes chase the data. Then try the eight blobs: GANs are notorious for dropping some of them.

\[ \begin{aligned} &\min_G \max_D\ V(D, G), \quad\text{where} \\ V &= \mathbb E_{x\sim p_{\text{data}}}\big[\log D(x)\big] \\ &\quad + \mathbb E_{z\sim p_z}\big[\log\big(1 - D(G(z))\big)\big] \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: D pushes V up: log D(x) reaches its best value, 0, when D says 1 on real points, and log(1 − D(G(z))) reaches 0 when D says 0 on fakes. Each D update is a step of logistic regression, real against fake. G pushes the same V down but can only touch the second term.
Say it“G minimises and D maximises the expected log D of real x plus the expected log of one minus D of G of z.”
\[ \mathcal L_G = -\,\mathbb E_{z\sim p_z}\big[\log D(G(z))\big] \]
Read it as: early in training D rejects every fake easily, so D(G(z)) ≈ 0, where log(1 − D) is nearly flat and G gets almost no gradient. Goodfellow’s fix, used by almost every GAN since: let G maximise log D(G(z)) instead. The goal is the same; the gradient is strong exactly when G is losing. This page trains G this way.
Say it“The generator’s loss is minus the expected log of D of G of z.”

modes found

Training instability

Why GANs are hard to train

Ordinary training walks downhill on one loss. A GAN is a game: each player walks downhill on its own loss, and every move reshapes the other player’s landscape. Gradient steps can then circle the solution for ever, or spiral away from it. The smallest example has one number per player: x wants the product x·y small, y wants it large. The only equilibrium is (0, 0), and plain gradient steps never reach it. Drag the starting point and switch the update rule.

\[ \begin{aligned} &\min_x \max_y\ f(x,y) = x\,y \\ &x_{k+1} = x_k - \eta\,y_k \\ &y_{k+1} = y_k + \eta\,x_k \\ &\Rightarrow\ r_{k+1} = \sqrt{1+\eta^2}\; r_k \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: both players follow their own gradient at the same time (∂f/∂x = y for the minimiser, ∂f/∂y = x for the maximiser). The update is a rotation plus a stretch, so the distance r from the equilibrium grows by √(1 + η²) at every step, for every learning rate η. Taking turns (alternating, as GAN code does) gives a closed orbit that never settles. The extragradient method first takes a trial step, then moves using the gradient found there, and spirals inwards by √(1 − η² + η⁴) per step.
Say it“x steps against y, y steps along x, and the radius grows by root one plus eta squared every step.”
distance from equilibrium at the end
growth factor per step

Real GANs fail in the same ways and a few more. They oscillate, as above. They suffer mode collapse: G finds a few outputs that fool the current D and piles all its samples there; D adapts, G jumps elsewhere, and the cycle repeats. And when D wins too clearly, G’s gradients vanish. A decade of fixes made GANs work in practice: the Wasserstein loss and its gradient penalty (Arjovsky et al., 2017; Gulrajani et al., 2017), spectral normalisation of D (Miyato et al., 2018), separate learning rates for the two players (Heusel et al., 2017), and very careful architectures such as StyleGAN (Karras et al., 2019). Diffusion models sidestep the game altogether.

Diffusion, step one

Adding noise, a little at a time

Diffusion models (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Ho, Jain & Abbeel, 2020) take the opposite route. There is no game, only a fixed recipe for destroying data and a network trained to reverse it. Each step of the forward process shrinks every point slightly towards the origin and adds a little Gaussian noise. After 100 steps nothing of the data is left: it has become a standard bell curve, exactly the noise we know how to sample. There is even a shortcut: xt can be drawn from x0 in a single jump. Slide the time t and watch the spiral dissolve.

\[ \begin{aligned} q(x_t \mid x_{t-1}) &= \mathcal N\big(\sqrt{1-\beta_t}\;x_{t-1}, \\ &\qquad\quad \beta_t I\big) \\ x_t &= \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\;x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\;\varepsilon \\ \bar\alpha_t &= \textstyle\prod_{s=1}^{t}(1-\beta_s) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: βt, the schedule, is the small amount of noise added at step t. Each step keeps √(1 − βt) of the signal, so data with variance 1 keeps variance 1. Multiply the shrink factors together and the whole chain collapses into one formula: ᾱt is the share of the original signal’s variance that survives to time t, and ε is one standard-normal draw. ᾱ0 = 1 is clean data; ᾱ100 ≈ 0 is pure noise.
Say it“x-t is root alpha-bar-t times x-nought, plus root one minus alpha-bar-t times epsilon.”
signal kept ᾱt
signal-to-noise ᾱ/(1 − ᾱ)

Diffusion, step two

The denoiser: guess the noise

To run the film backwards we need, at every t, an answer to one question: given a noisy point xt, what noise was added? Train a network εθ(xt, t) on exactly that. Take a real point, noise it to a random time, and score the network’s guess of ε by squared error. A guess of the noise is also a guess of the clean point, and a direction in which to move. For the spiral, the best possible guess can be computed exactly, so we can see what a perfect denoiser does. Drag the probe (the ringed dot) and change t.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal L(\theta) &= \mathbb E_{x_0,\,t,\,\varepsilon}\,\big\Vert \varepsilon - \varepsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\big\Vert^2 \\ x_t &= \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: Ho et al.’s “simple” loss, averaged over real points x0, random times t and random noise ε. It is plain regression, with no adversary, which is why diffusion training is so stable. The best possible εθ is the average of all the noises that could have produced xt.
Say it“The loss is the expected squared distance between the true noise and the network’s guess of it.”
\[ \begin{aligned} \hat x_0 &= \frac{x_t - \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\;\hat\varepsilon}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}} \\ \nabla_x \log p_t(x_t) &= -\frac{\hat\varepsilon}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: solve the forward formula for x0 to turn a noise guess ε̂ into a clean guess x̂0. With the best ε̂, x̂0 is the average of every clean point that could have produced xt (Tweedie’s formula), and −ε̂ points uphill on the noisy data’s density: it is the score. That is why diffusion models are also called score-based models (Song & Ermon, 2019).
Say it“x-nought-hat is x-t minus root one minus alpha-bar times epsilon-hat, all over root alpha-bar.”
clean guess x̂0
spiral points still in the running

Diffusion, step three

Sampling: running the noise backwards

Now generate. Start from pure noise at t = 100. At each step, remove a little of the noise the network predicts and add back a little fresh noise, until t = 0. Here the denoiser is a real network (three hidden layers of 64 units, about 9,700 weights), and you train it live: press Train, then Sample, and compare its samples with those of the exact denoiser from the last section. The deterministic DDIM sampler (Song, Meng & Ermon, 2021) adds no fresh noise and can take big strides: try 10 steps instead of 100.

\[ \begin{aligned} x_{t-1} &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Big(x_t - \frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\,\hat\varepsilon\Big) \\ &\quad + \sigma_t z \\ \alpha_t &= 1-\beta_t \\ \sigma_t^2 &= \beta_t\,\frac{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}{1-\bar\alpha_t} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: DDPM, one step back. Subtract the predicted noise, scaled for one step, and undo the shrink; then add fresh noise z ~ N(0, I) of size σt (none at the last step). The jiggle keeps samples varied. 100 steps means 100 network evaluations per sample: the price of diffusion. A GAN pays 1. (The code here, like most image code, takes the step through the clean guess x̂0 and clips it to the data’s range; that changes only the first, noisiest steps.)
Say it“x-t-minus-one is one over root alpha-t times x-t minus beta-t over root one minus alpha-bar-t times epsilon-hat, plus sigma-t z.”
\[ \begin{aligned} x_{s} &= \sqrt{\bar\alpha_{s}}\;\hat x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{s}}\;\hat\varepsilon \\ &\text{for any earlier time } s < t \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: DDIM. Guess the clean point x̂0 from ε̂ (previous section), then jump straight to any earlier time s by re-noising that guess with the same noise ε̂ instead of fresh noise. No randomness after the start, so it can skip steps: one noise draw always gives the same sample.
Say it“x-s is root alpha-bar-s times x-nought-hat plus root one minus alpha-bar-s times epsilon-hat.”

Guided generation

Guidance: asking for something

An unconditional model draws from all of the data. To ask for something specific (a digit 7, a photo of a cat, “an astronaut riding a horse”), hand the denoiser the request too: εθ(xt, t, c). Ho & Salimans (2021) found a way to make the request count for more. Train one network that sometimes sees the label and sometimes does not, then at sampling time push its prediction away from the unconditional one. Below, three overlapping classes share the plane, and their exact denoisers are known. Pick a class and raise the guidance w.

\[ \begin{aligned} \tilde\varepsilon &= (1+w)\,\hat\varepsilon(x_t, t, c) \\ &\quad - w\,\hat\varepsilon(x_t, t, \varnothing) \\ -\frac{\tilde\varepsilon}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}} &= \nabla \log p_t(x_t \mid c) \\ &\quad + w\,\nabla \log p_t(c \mid x_t) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: classifier-free guidance. ∅ means “no label”. w = 0 is plain conditional sampling. By Bayes’ rule, w > 0 adds w times the gradient of an implicit classifier, pushing samples towards places where the class is unmistakable. Samples become more typical and less varied: the fidelity–diversity trade-off that every text-to-image system tunes. (Stable Diffusion’s default “guidance scale” of 7.5 multiplies the conditional term by 7.5, which is w = 6.5 here.)
Say it“Epsilon-tilde is one plus w times the conditional guess, minus w times the unconditional guess.”
samples a perfect classifier calls the requested class
spread of the samples (real data: 0.70)

Choosing

GAN, VAE or diffusion?

From 2014 to about 2020 GANs made the most realistic images; StyleGAN’s faces are still hard to tell from photographs. Then Dhariwal & Nichol (2021) showed diffusion models beating GANs on ImageNet, and latent diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022), which runs the diffusion in an autoencoder’s compressed space, became Stable Diffusion. Each family makes a different trade.

Real-world project

Project: handwritten digits out of noise

The UCI Optical Recognition of Handwritten Digits data (Alpaydin & Kaynak, 1998) holds 5,620 digits written on forms by 43 people, scanned and reduced to 8×8 grids of ink counts from 0 to 16. Its official split is by writer: 3,823 digits from 30 writers to train on and 1,797 from 13 other writers to test on. A diffusion model was trained offline in numpy on the training writers only: an MLP with three hidden layers of 256 units that takes the noisy image, the time t and the digit label, and predicts the noise ( weights, embedded in this page). During training the label was hidden 15% of the time, so the same network also works unconditionally, which is what classifier-free guidance needs. Everything below runs in your browser.

Real digits by the 13 test writers, never seen in training.

1 · Step through the reverse process

Choose a digit and a guidance strength, then step from noise at t = 100 down to a finished digit at t = 0. At every step the network’s noise guess gives a clean guess x̂0 (clipped to the ink range, as image diffusion code does), and an independent classifier, a logistic regression trained on the same 3,823 digits, says what that guess looks like.

Digit to draw

2 · A sheet of samples, and the price of guidance

Generate four of every digit with the same noise seeds and check them two ways. Does the classifier read each sample as the digit that was asked for? And is each sample new, or a copy of a training digit? For the second question, compare each sample’s distance to its nearest training digit with the same distance for the real test digits, which are new handwriting by definition.

read as the digit asked for

The same model in numpy

import json, numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

def load(f):                                         # UCI optdigits: 64 ink counts (0..16) + label
    D = np.loadtxt(f, delimiter=",", dtype=int); return D[:, :64], D[:, 64]
Xtr, ytr = load("optdigits.tra")                     # 3,823 digits, 30 writers
Xte, yte = load("optdigits.tes")                     # 1,797 digits, 13 other writers
s = lambda X: X / 16 * 2 - 1                         # ink to [-1, 1]

M = np.load("gd_model.npz")                          # trained offline (gd-train.py), stored as float16
W = [M[f"W{l}"].astype(np.float64) for l in range(4)]; b = [M[f"b{l}"].astype(np.float64) for l in range(4)]
AB, BE, FREQ, T = M["AB"], M["BE"], M["FREQ"], 100

def eps_hat(x, t, c):                                # x: (n, 64); t: int; c: digit 0..9 or -1 for "no label"
    a = t / T * FREQ
    h = np.hstack([x, np.tile(np.r_[np.sin(a), np.cos(a)], (len(x), 1)), np.zeros((len(x), 10))])
    if c >= 0: h[:, 96 + c] = 1
    for l in range(3):
        z = h @ W[l] + b[l]; h = z / (1 + np.exp(-z))  # SiLU
    return h @ W[3] + b[3]

def mulberry32(a):                                   # the page's random numbers, bit for bit
    def r():
        nonlocal a
        a = (a + 0x6D2B79F5) & 0xFFFFFFFF; t = a
        t = ((t ^ (t >> 15)) * (t | 1)) & 0xFFFFFFFF
        t ^= (t + (((t ^ (t >> 7)) * (t | 61)) & 0xFFFFFFFF)) & 0xFFFFFFFF
        return ((t ^ (t >> 14)) & 0xFFFFFFFF) / 4294967296
    return r
def gauss(r):
    u = 0
    while u == 0: u = r()
    return np.sqrt(-2 * np.log(u)) * np.cos(2 * np.pi * r())

def sample(seed, c, w):                              # DDPM, 100 steps, classifier-free guidance w
    r = mulberry32(seed); x = np.array([[gauss(r) for _ in range(64)]])
    for t in range(T, 0, -1):
        e = eps_hat(x, t, c) if c < 0 or w == 0 else (1 + w) * eps_hat(x, t, c) - w * eps_hat(x, t, -1)
        x0 = np.clip((x - np.sqrt(1 - AB[t]) * e) / np.sqrt(AB[t]), -1, 1)
        x = (np.sqrt(AB[t - 1]) * BE[t] * x0 + np.sqrt(1 - BE[t]) * (1 - AB[t - 1]) * x) / (1 - AB[t])
        if t > 1: x = x + np.sqrt(BE[t] * (1 - AB[t - 1]) / (1 - AB[t])) * np.array([[gauss(r) for _ in range(64)]])
    return x0[0]

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)                       # denoising loss, same t and noise for both sets
for name, X in (("training writers", Xtr), ("test writers", Xte)):
    t = rng.integers(1, T + 1, len(X)); e = rng.standard_normal((len(X), 64)); L = []
    for tt in range(1, T + 1):
        k = t == tt; xt = np.sqrt(AB[tt]) * s(X[k]) + np.sqrt(1 - AB[tt]) * e[k]
        L.append(((eps_hat(xt, tt, -1) - e[k]) ** 2).sum())
    print(f"noise-prediction loss, {name:16s}: {sum(L) / X.size:.4f}")

clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000).fit(s(Xtr), ytr)
cW, cb = np.round(clf.coef_, 5), np.round(clf.intercept_, 5)
read = lambda X: (s(X) @ cW.T + cb).argmax(1)       # the independent judge
print(f"classifier accuracy on the test writers: {(read(Xte) == yte).mean():.4f}")
nn = lambda X: np.sqrt(((X[:, None, :] - Xtr[None]) ** 2).sum(2)).min(1)
print(f"test digits: median distance to nearest training digit {np.median(nn(Xte)):.2f}")

x = sample(7, 3, 1.0)                                # the page's first sample: seed 7, digit 3, w = 1
print("seed 7, digit 3, w = 1, first 8 pixels:", np.round((x[:8] + 1) * 8, 4))
sheet = {}
for w in (0, 1, 2, 3, 4):                            # the page's sheet: 4 of each digit, seeds 100..139
    G = np.array([(sample(100 + k, k % 10, w) + 1) * 8 for k in range(40)])
    ok = (read(G) == np.arange(40) % 10).mean(); d = np.median(nn(G)); sheet[w] = [ok, d]
    print(f"w = {w}: sheet of 40, read as the digit asked for {ok:.3f}, median distance to nearest training digit {d:.2f}")
json.dump({"x7": list(x), "sheet": sheet, "cW": cW.T.ravel().tolist(), "cb": cb.tolist()}, open("gd_ref.json", "w"))

Wrap-up

Five lines to remember

  • A generator is a learned map from easy noise to data: x = G(z). Where it stretches, probability thins; where it squeezes, probability piles up.
  • A GAN trains G against a discriminator D. With the best D, the game’s value is −log 4 + 2 JSD, so fooling D means matching the data. G trains on −log D(G(z)) to keep its gradients alive.
  • Two players doing gradient steps can circle or spiral instead of converging: that, plus mode collapse and vanishing gradients, is why GANs are hard to train.
  • Diffusion destroys data with a fixed noise schedule, xt = √ᾱt x0 + √(1−ᾱt) ε, trains a network to predict ε by plain regression, and samples by removing the predicted noise step by step.
  • Classifier-free guidance, (1+w) ε̂(x, c) − w ε̂(x, ∅), makes samples more clearly what you asked for and less varied.

Check your understanding

At the end of perfect GAN training, what does the discriminator output, and what is its loss?

D*(x) = pdata/(pdata + pG) = 1/2 everywhere, because pG = pdata. Its loss, −log D(x) − log(1 − D(G(z))), is then 2 ln 2 ≈ 1.386, and the value V is −log 4.

Why does the generator usually minimise −log D(G(z)) rather than log(1 − D(G(z)))?

Both are lowest when D(G(z)) = 1, but early on D(G(z)) ≈ 0, where log(1 − D) is nearly flat: G would learn almost nothing. −log D(G(z)) is steep exactly there.

A GAN trained on the eight blobs puts all its samples on three of them, and D’s loss looks healthy. What is happening, and what might help?

Mode collapse: G has found outputs that fool the current D and ignores the rest of the data. A healthy-looking loss does not reveal it; you have to look at the samples or measure coverage. A Wasserstein loss with gradient penalty, spectral normalisation, minibatch statistics or simply a different learning rate balance can help. Or use a diffusion model.

At some time t the signal kept is ᾱ = 0.25. Write the noisy point in terms of the clean point x₀ and the noise ε. How much of the variance is noise?

xt = 0.5 x0 + √0.75 ε ≈ 0.5 x0 + 0.866 ε. For unit-variance data, 75% of the variance is noise; the signal-to-noise ratio is 0.25/0.75 = 1/3.

Raising the guidance w makes every generated 7 look like a textbook 7. What has been lost?

Diversity. Guidance adds w times the gradient of log p(c | x), pulling samples to where the class is unmistakable and away from unusual but valid ways of writing a 7. Too much guidance also pushes samples past the data into exaggerated, over-saturated images.
